lesson.title: Counting Cognates Gym
lesson.subtitle: Phone numbers, prices, ages — and the elf ≠ elf trap

hook.title: Numbers in the Wild
hook.content: You own the shift-ledger numbers — now spend them. Prices: Das kostet zwölf Euro. Ages: Ich bin dreißig. Time: Es ist acht Uhr. Phone numbers, read digit by digit: zwei–null–eins... And the trap that snags every learner at once: elf means eleven — but there is also die Elfe, the fairy, a modern borrowing from English elf. Same letters, different words, different genders. In the wild, context decides; in this gym, reps decide.

footnotes.title: Zwo — the Anti-Mishear
footnotes.content: On the phone and in radio traffic, Germans often say zwo for zwei — because zwei and drei differ by one sound and mix-ups cost lives on the autobahn. Pilots and the Bundeswehr say zwo too. two got a stunt double.

pattern.title: Spend the Numbers
pattern.content: Prices: Das kostet zwanzig Euro — Euro is the same word in both languages. Ages: Ich bin dreißig Jahre alt (Jahre — year, the distant cousin of Uhr via the same PIE root). Clock: Es ist sieben Uhr — sieben is the v→b twin of seven, acht the gh→ch twin of eight. Compound numbers: einundzwanzig (21, where 'one' becomes ein-), zweiundzwanzig, dreiundzwanzig — the ones ALWAYS lead, reading like 'three-and-twenty'.
pattern.linguist_note: The ein- of einundzwanzig shows the ein-family doing number duty — the same ein as 'one/a'. English 'one' and German ein are twins; the article was always a number that got tired of counting.

exercises.prompt: Match the number words with their English twins:
exercises.explanation: seven's v hardened to b, eight's gh became ch, elf kept its 'one-left', dreißig double-shifted — and the counting verb counts itself in: zählen, tale's twin, zählt die Zeit und bis hundert.

exercises.prompt: Trap check: 'Die Elfe tanzt im Garten.' What is dancing?
options: A fairy (die Elfe — the borrowed creature-word)
exercises.target_answer: A fairy (die Elfe — the borrowed creature-word)
exercises.explanation: The number elf has no article; the fairy die Elfe was borrowed from English 'elf' in the 18th century. Context and article decide.
drei + und + zwanzig — 'three-and-twenty', the archaic English order, written as one word. Minutes follow the same arithmetic: eine Minute, zwanzig Minuten — one always leads the line.

exercises.english_hint: the double-shift number with the ß
exercises.meaning: Ich bin dreißig = I am thirty
exercises.explanation: dreißig — drei's th→d plus thirty's t→ß. The only number that spelled its shift. Moving day runs on the clock too: um acht Uhr wollen wir ausziehen.

vocab_hints.note: die Kosten — the costs; the -et is the er-form ending on a stem that ends in -t

exercises.explanation: Verb in position 2, price at the end: 'Der Bus kostet zwanzig Euro' — der Bus and Euro are your free cognates.

summary.outcome: Use numbers for prices, ages, clock time — and survive the elf/Elfe trap.
summary.takeaway: Numbers are shift-ledger words — and German says 23 as 'three-and-twenty', ones first, always.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: Days of Thunder — the weekday etymologies of Donner, Mitte and Sonne in one calendar.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Counting Cognates Gym (The bus costs twenty euros):
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Der Bus kostet zwanzig Euro" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Counting Cognates Gym without relying on short-term echo.

zwanzig.etymology_derivation: zwei + -zig (German's ancient -ty, as in six-ty); the whole word is a double t → z shift of twenty. [wiktionary]

elf.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *ainalif — 'one left over' after counting ten, the exact twin of eleven. [wiktionary]

zwölf.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *twalif — 'two left over', the exact tw → zw twin of twelve. [wiktionary]

dreißig.shift_rule: TH → D + T → S / SS / Z
dreißig.etymology_derivation: drei + the old -zig ending (English's -ty): thirty with th → d and t → ß — a double-shift number. [wiktionary]

uhr.etymology_derivation: Loan-cognate of hour (Latin hōra via French), and a distant doublet of Jahr and year (PIE *yóh₁r̥). German alone turned it into the word for the clock itself. [wiktionary]

hundert.context_phrase: Ein Jahr hat nicht hundert Tage.
hundert.context_translation: A year does not have a hundred days.
hundert.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hundaradą 'hundred-count' — the twin of English hundred. [wiktionary]

minute.etymology_derivation: Medieval Latin minūta — the same Latin loan as English minute. [wiktionary]

zählen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *taljaną, the causative of the tal-root — the same family as English tell and tale; the initial t became z, as in two, zwei. [wiktionary]

mahlzeit.context_phrase: Wir essen drei Mahlzeiten am Tag.
mahlzeit.context_translation: We eat three meals a day.
mahlzeit.etymology_derivation: Mahlzeit — Mahl (meal) plus Zeit (time); Wiktionary compares English mealtide, so Mahl is a direct cognate of meal and Zeit of tide, whose t became z in German. [wiktionary]

jahreszeit.context_phrase: Es gibt vier Jahreszeiten im Jahr.
jahreszeit.context_translation: There are four seasons in a year.
jahreszeit.etymology_derivation: Jahr + Zeit — year-time; Jahr is the twin of English year and Zeit the twin of tide, which originally meant time. [wiktionary]

russisch.etymology_derivation: Russe + the suffix -isch, the twin of English -ish; the Rus name reached German via Medieval Latin Russus from Greek Rhos. [wiktionary]

grüßen.context_phrase: Ich grüße meine Nachbarin jeden Morgen.
grüßen.context_translation: I greet my neighbor every morning.
grüßen.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *grōtijan — English greet is the documented cognate; the old t hissed to ß in German (the sibilant shift). [wiktionary]

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Described by Walter Skeat as the primary dental affrication and spirantization of High German.
